# Appendix — Microsoft How-To Implementation References
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Download this appendix
**[appendix-microsoft-howto.docx](appendix-microsoft-howto.docx)** — this entire appendix as a single Word document. Regenerated on every site deploy.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
This appendix is the tactical *how* companion to the strategic *why + sequencing*
in the books. Each section gives the authoritative Microsoft Learn link and the
core implementation steps for one capability, then points back to the book that
reasons about it. It introduces no new doctrine; it operationalizes
[ADR-091](../../adr/adr-091-sql-server-authentication-transformation.qmd) and
[ADR-068](../../adr/adr-068-kerberos-ntlm-elimination.qmd) (both **PROPOSED**),
which remain the governing decisions.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Scope — on-premises SQL Server enabled by Azure Arc
Every step below targets the **on-premises SQL Server engine enabled by Azure
Arc** — SQL Server 2022 (16.x) or later running on a Windows Server host in your
data center. It is **not** Azure SQL Database or Azure SQL Managed Instance. This
distinction matters most for connection strings: the server endpoint is your own
host (`tcp:<sqlhost>.<domain>,1433`), **never** a `*.database.windows.net`
endpoint. Microsoft's connection-string articles are written against Azure SQL
and use `*.database.windows.net` in their examples — the `Authentication=...`
keywords carry over unchanged, but the server address does not.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Production safety (GCC-Moderate / FedRAMP)
The steps that create logins, configure the engine, or change NTLM Group Policy
alter a production security posture. Treat every such step as **review-required**:
run discovery and audit read-only first, capture the planned change, and route it
through your environment's change-control and security review before enforcement.
Validate each step against your GCC-Moderate boundary requirements (proxy,
private endpoints, policy initiatives) — several of the details below differ
inside a restricted boundary, and those differences are called out where they
occur.
:::

## 1. Azure Arc enablement + SQL Server extension (the identity bridge)

**Companion to:** [Book 04 — the Arc identity bridge](Book_04.qmd).

**Primary Microsoft documentation:**

- [SQL Server enabled by Azure Arc — overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/sql-server/azure-arc/overview)
- [Set up Microsoft Entra authentication with app registration for SQL Server](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/authentication-access/azure-ad-authentication-sql-server-setup-tutorial)

**Core implementation steps:**

1. **Install the Azure Connected Machine agent** on the Windows Server host
   (Windows Server 2019+ supported). Ensure outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) to the Arc
   endpoints (`management.azure.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, and the Arc
   data-service endpoints). A proxy is supported for GCC-Moderate boundaries.
2. **Register the server in Azure Arc.** This creates the ARM resource and the
   host's **system-assigned managed identity**.
3. **Install the Azure extension for SQL Server** (recommended via Azure Policy
   for fleet scale; requires SQL Server 2022+). The SQL Server 2022 setup wizard
   does not install the extension — install it from the command line or by
   connecting the server to Arc.
4. **Provision the app registration and certificate.** Entra authentication for
   Arc-enabled SQL Server requires a **Microsoft Entra app registration**
   (granted `User.Read.All`, `GroupMember.Read.All` / `Application.Read.All` or
   `Directory.Read.All`) **and a certificate stored in Azure Key Vault**. The Arc
   agent downloads the certificate to the host; the engine uses it to query Entra
   ID on behalf of the instance. This is the actual crux of setup — not an
   optional extra. (See §2.)
5. **Verify the managed identity and agent health.** Confirm the agent is
   connected with `azcmagent show`, and confirm the extension is healthy and the
   managed identity is active under the Arc SQL resource in the Azure portal.
   The Arc managed-identity token is served from the local IMDS endpoint on port
   `40342`, but it is **not** a plain GET: the endpoint requires a `Metadata:true`
   header and a challenge/response against a local secret file, so use the agent
   tooling or the Azure Identity libraries (which perform that handshake) rather
   than a bare `curl`.

::: {.callout-note}
## GCC-Moderate proxy correction
Microsoft Entra authentication **does not use the Arc Connected Machine agent's
proxy setting** for its calls to Entra ID. Inside a boundary that forces egress
through a proxy, you must set the **machine-level WinHTTP proxy** separately:

```console
netsh winhttp set proxy proxy-server="proxyserver:port"
```

Setting only the Arc agent proxy (`azcmagent config set proxy.url ...`) covers
the agent's own traffic but leaves Entra authentication unable to reach
`login.microsoftonline.com`. This is a common GCC-Moderate failure mode.
:::

**Layer distinction (Microsoft alignment):** SQL Server *engine* Entra
authentication (this program) works on a domain-joined host. Full *OS-level*
Entra logon (RDP with Entra credentials) is a separate, later layer that requires
domain unjoin and a newer Windows Server baseline — see
[ADR-002](../../adr/adr-002-arc-entra-join-no-domain-join.qmd). Do not conflate
the two: you do **not** need to unjoin the host to give the SQL engine Entra
authentication.

## 2. Enable Microsoft Entra authentication on SQL Server

**Companion to:** [Book 04](Book_04.qmd) and [Book 05](Book_05.qmd).

**Primary Microsoft documentation:**

- [Microsoft Entra authentication for SQL Server — overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/authentication-access/azure-ad-authentication-sql-server-overview)
- [Tutorial: set up Microsoft Entra authentication for SQL Server](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/authentication-access/azure-ad-authentication-sql-server-setup-tutorial)

**Core steps:**

- The Arc Connected Machine agent **and** the Azure extension for SQL Server must
  be deployed first (§1), along with the app registration and Key Vault
  certificate.
- In the Azure portal → the **SQL Server – Azure Arc** resource →
  **Microsoft Entra ID and Purview** → **Set Admin**. Choose the customer-managed
  certificate and the customer-managed app registration created in §1, then
  **Save**. This designates the first Entra admin (a user or group granted
  server-level `sysadmin`). *This portal flow applies to SQL Server 2022 (16.x);
  SQL Server 2025 (17.x) configures the admin differently — follow the
  version-selected guidance in the tutorial.*
- SQL Server 2022 or later is required; failover cluster instances are not
  supported for Entra authentication.
- **Without Azure Arc** (not recommended for this program): Microsoft documents a
  separate "enable Microsoft Entra authentication for SQL Server on Windows
  without Azure Arc" path that still requires an app registration, a certificate,
  and host registry configuration — it is not a single registry toggle. Prefer
  the Arc path, which manages the certificate lifecycle for you.

---

## 3. `CREATE LOGIN ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER` (Entra logins)

**Companion to:** [Book 05 — login migration & parallel-run validation](Book_05.qmd).

**Primary Microsoft documentation:**

- [CREATE LOGIN (Transact-SQL)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/create-login-transact-sql)

**Syntax examples** (run in the `master` database):

```sql
-- Entra user (principal name is the user principal name)
CREATE LOGIN [user@contoso.com] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;

-- Entra security group (principal name is the group's display name)
CREATE LOGIN [DBA-Team-Prod] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;

-- Entra service principal / application (principal name is the app's display name)
CREATE LOGIN [MyApp-ServicePrincipal] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;
```

**Database user mapping** (run in the target database):

```sql
CREATE USER [user@contoso.com] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;
ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [user@contoso.com];
```

**Granting a server role** (e.g. `sysadmin`) uses `ALTER SERVER ROLE`, run in
`master`:

```sql
ALTER SERVER ROLE sysadmin ADD MEMBER [admin@contoso.com];
```

**Notes:**

- The login name must match the Entra **user principal name** for users, or the
  Entra **object's name** for groups and service principals.
- No password is stored. Authentication occurs via an Entra-issued OAuth 2.0
  access token validated by the engine.
- List Entra principals with `SELECT * FROM sys.server_principals WHERE type IN
  ('E','X');` (`E` = external user, `X` = external group/application).

## 4. Application connection-string migration

**Companion to:** [Book 08 — the upstream application chain](Book_08.qmd).

**Primary Microsoft documentation:**

- [Connect with Microsoft Entra authentication using SqlClient](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/ado-net/sql/azure-active-directory-authentication)

The `Authentication=...` keywords below come from the SqlClient article, which is
written for Azure SQL. **Point `Server` at your on-premises Arc-enabled host, not
a `*.database.windows.net` endpoint.**

- **Managed identity** (app runs on an Azure or Arc-enabled host with a managed
  identity):

  ```
  Server=tcp:sqlhost.contoso.com,1433;Database=YourDB;Encrypt=True;Authentication=Active Directory Managed Identity;
  ```

- **Default credential chain** (recommended for dev/prod consistency; resolves
  managed identity, Azure CLI, Visual Studio, etc. via `DefaultAzureCredential`):

  ```
  Server=tcp:sqlhost.contoso.com,1433;Database=YourDB;Encrypt=True;Authentication=Active Directory Default;
  ```

- **Service principal** (client ID + secret):

  ```
  Server=tcp:sqlhost.contoso.com,1433;Database=YourDB;Encrypt=True;Authentication=Active Directory Service Principal;User Id=<appId>;Password=<secret>;
  ```

**.NET code example** (`DefaultAzureCredential` chain; on an Arc host this
resolves the managed identity through the Arc IMDS handshake automatically):

```csharp
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;

// Authentication=Active Directory Default lets the driver acquire the token via
// DefaultAzureCredential — no credential object is constructed by the app.
using var connection = new SqlConnection(
    "Server=tcp:sqlhost.contoso.com,1433;Database=YourDB;Encrypt=True;" +
    "Authentication=Active Directory Default;");
await connection.OpenAsync();
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 7.0 package change
Starting with **Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 7.0**, the Entra ID authentication modes
(`Active Directory Default`, `Active Directory Managed Identity`, etc.) are no
longer in the core package. If your application uses any of them, add the
**`Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.Extensions.Azure`** NuGet package — otherwise the
driver raises an actionable error at connect time. No connection-string changes
are needed beyond adding the reference.
:::

Entra-authenticated connections are always encrypted (`Encrypt=True`); if the
server uses a self-signed certificate you must also add `TrustServerCertificate=True`
or, preferably, deploy a trusted TLS certificate. This pattern eliminates stored
credentials from connection strings and configuration files.

## 5. NTLM elimination & hardening

**Companion to:** [Book 06 — NTLM elimination at the SQL layer](Book_06.qmd).

**Primary Microsoft documentation:**

- [Network security: Restrict NTLM — NTLM authentication in this domain](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-restrict-ntlm-ntlm-authentication-in-this-domain)
- [Network security: LAN Manager authentication level](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-lan-manager-authentication-level)

**Key actions, aligned to the program phases:**

- **Fix missing or incorrect SPNs** so Kerberos is negotiated instead of falling
  back to NTLM:

  ```
  setspn -S MSSQLSvc/hostname.domain.com:port serviceaccount
  ```

- **Group Policy — LAN Manager authentication level:** set *Network security: LAN
  Manager authentication level* to **Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM**
  (registry `LmCompatibilityLevel` = 5). This refuses LM and NTLM and accepts only
  NTLMv2.
- **Group Policy — Restrict NTLM (domain controllers):** before denying, set the
  matching **Audit NTLM authentication in this domain** policy first, review the
  operational log under *Applications and Services Log\\Microsoft\\Windows\\NTLM*,
  build a server-exception list, then move to a **Deny** option. Restricting
  before auditing is how productivity-breaking outages happen.
- **Migrate to Entra tokens** (type-E logins, §3) or Cloud Kerberos Trust where a
  Kerberos path is still required.
- **Monitor** with Windows Event IDs 4624 / 4625 (Logon Type 3, NTLM package) and
  the dedicated NTLM operational log above.

**SQL-specific outcome:** once an instance is migrated to Entra (type-E) logins,
its connections use Entra OAuth 2.0 tokens and generate zero NTLM traffic — which
is what the CCM-BIR closure record in [Book 09](Book_09.qmd) confirms per
instance.

## How to use this appendix

- Read each section alongside the book it points to — the book carries the
  reasoning, sequencing, and the shipped UIAO automation; this appendix carries
  the Microsoft links and the minimal step list.
- The UIAO discovery and assessment tooling (the `Spec*-D1.*` family and the
  `UIAOSqlServerMigration` module) provides program-level governance —
  estate inventory, reconciliation, the CCM-BIR closure record and drift diff —
  that goes beyond Microsoft's general-purpose tools (Azure Migrate, Defender for
  SQL). The Microsoft steps here are the per-host mechanics; the UIAO tooling is
  the fleet-level control loop over them.
- Microsoft Learn content changes; the linked articles carry the current,
  version-selected detail. Where this appendix and a linked article disagree,
  the article wins — open an issue so this page can be reconciled.
